00:00:05 - Ava (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick 30 minute sync, focus on throughput numbers and action items. carlos, maya, priya, can you hear me ok?

00:00:30 - Liam (Redwood): quick agenda: one, review latest benchmark we ran Friday; two, tuning recommendations around continuous batching and concurrency; three, plan for a 24 hour mixed workload test; four, infra deep-dive next week.sound good?
00:00:42 - Carlos: yes, sounds good. we really want to see stable p95 under 450ms and cost under our threshold, so that'll be the success criteria.
00:00:55 - Ava: noted. we had p95 around 430ms on the shorter prompt set at concurrency 8, tokens per second looked good, but with the mixed workload p95 spiked to ~820ms on tail.

00:01:20 - Maya: can you clarify what you mean by mixed workload? our real traffic is a lot of multi-turn chat with occasional long completions.
00:01:28 - Liam: yeah, mixed means a blend of short chat turns (~16-50 tokens) and longer generation (~400-1200 tokens) at roughly 70/30 split, which causes fragmentation in batching and KV cache misses.
\00:01:50 - Carlos: i think that explains the tail. the p50 was fine but p95 killed us.

00:02:05 - Liam: right. our first knob is continuous batching window — increasing the window from 20ms to 50ms improved batching efficiency in our microbench, throughput up ~18% but latency p95 increased slightly if concurrency remained high. there's a tradeoff.
00:02:28 - Priya: wait, so bigger window helps tokens/sec but hurts latency tail sometimes?
00:02:33 - Liam: exactly, because you let more requests coalesce into larger batches which is more GPU-efficient, but individual requests wait longer in queue. however, if we also tune concurrency (number of in-flight requests) we can often get the best of both worlds.

00:02:50 - Ava: we proposed a concurrency target strategy: keep concurrency low for long-generation-heavy routes, and higher concurrency for short-turn routes. also route by cost/latency policy so we can fallback to a smaller model if tail gets bad.
00:03:07 - Maya: is model fallback something we can do during POC? we want to keep quality stable.
00:03:12 - Ava: we can configure automatic fallback to a quantized variant with a quick warm KV cache, but we'll share evals so you can confirm quality diffs.

00:03:30 - Ethan (SRE): on the infra side, our worry is queue blowup if a downstream spike happens. how do you handle queue limits?
00:03:38 - Liam: we have configurable queueing thresholds and soft/hard limits. soft limit applies backpressure to clients (429-ish) and hard limit drops or routes to a cheaper pool. queueing policies were in the doc i posted — i'll re-share that.

00:03:58 - Carlos: the doc looked good but could you call out the behavior during GPU OOMs?
00:04:03 - Liam: yeah, OOMs trigger immediate fallback at the per-model worker level and we drain the queue and fall back to a compatible variant; these events are rare in the POC since we've been using shorter seq lengths, but we'll add explicit notes.

00:04:25 - Ava: okay, benchmark review. liam, can you run through the spreadsheet highlights?
00:04:29 - Liam: sure. i shared the benchmark link — public sheet, redacted — quick takeaways: scenario A (short-turn only) at concurrency 16 gave 2.4k tokens/sec and p95 210ms; scenario B (mixed workload) at concurrency 8 had 1.1k tokens/sec but p95 820ms. increasing batching window improved tokens/sec to 1.3k but tail only modestly improved when we increased concurrency to 12.
00:05:05 - Maya: can you say which hardware these runs were on?
00:05:08 - Liam: all runs on r-infer-prod gpus, 4xA100 equivalent cluster, single-model worker w/ continuous batching enabled. we also tested a quantized variant on T4-like infra for cost sim.
00:05:24 - Priya: what's the impact on cost if we bump concurrency to 12? our cost model is per GPU hour and per token, so larger concurrency might require more instances.
00:05:33 - Liam: concurrency by itself doesn't allocate more GPUs — it's in-flight requests per worker. if throughput increases and you need more capacity, you'll autoscale by target tokens/sec or CPU/GPU utilization. so cost increases if you autoscale, but per-token cost actually drops because of batch efficiency.
00:05:52 - Carlos: mhm, cheaper per token but total spend might go up if traffic grows. we need to simulate production shape.

00:06:10 - Ava: this week we tested prefix caching for the top 50 prompts and saw hit rate ~26% which shaved 15% off tokens/sec cost in the short-turn scenario. that helps tail too because warmed KV reduces computation per request.
00:06:27 - Maya: top 50 prompts are mostly auth flows and account summaries; good candidate. how do you handle cache invalidation?
00:06:33 - Liam: configurable TTLs and explicit purge via API — also safe mode for sensitive prompts where we don't cache.

00:06:45 - Ethan: will caching store any PII? we have compliance concerns.
00:06:49 - Ava: by default prefix caching stores model KV state not raw user content; it's computed from tokenized input and we can disable for routes flagged as pii. plus we support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest.

00:07:05 - Carlos: social question: when you say KV cache, sometimes our docs call it KV cash, ha. the transcription in the sheet had some typos, just a heads up.
00:07:12 - Liam: yep, the demo recordings always have the classic 'cash' autocorrect, we've seen that.

00:07:34 - Liam: yes i'll kick that off tonight, will run mixed workload at three concurrency settings (8,12,16) and record p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec, and we'll include GPU utilization.
00:07:47 - Priya: please include end-to-end latency from our client side as well, i.e. including network times — that matters.

00:09:16 - Liam: yes, routing rules can be per-customer or per-route, you can set latency SLOs, cost budgets, and fallback model lists. it's all configurable via the control plane.
00:09:28 - Priya: are there hard limits for concurrent sessions per user? we'll have a lot of agents hitting at the same time.
00:09:33 - Liam: you can set per-API-key concurrency quotas and token quotas to protect from thundering herd.
00:09:45 - Carlos: okay, shifting to quality: if we use a quantized variant as fallback, what's the expected quality drop?
00:09:52 - Ava: small in most tasks; we'll provide eval comparisons on the prompts you share. for certain sensitive tasks we recommend no-fallback.
